expectedText:
MUTUAL NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · Beta Ventures, LLC

CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION, DEFINED RECIPROCALLY
Either Acme, Inc. or Beta Ventures, LLC may be the party disclosing information (the "Disclosing Party") or the party receiving it (the "Receiving Party") under this agreement, and that role can switch depending on which direction information is flowing at a given time. Each party's confidential information includes any business, technical, financial, or other information that party discloses to the other and marks or otherwise identifies as confidential, or that a reasonable person would understand to be confidential given its nature and the circumstances of disclosure. This definition and the protections that go with it apply equally regardless of which party is disclosing and which is receiving at that time.

RECIPROCAL CONFIDENTIALITY OBLIGATIONS
Each of Acme, Inc. and Beta Ventures, LLC will keep the other's confidential information private, use it only for the purpose of evaluating a potential business partnership, and take reasonable care to prevent anyone else from accessing it. These duties run in both directions on identical terms: whichever party is the Receiving Party at a given time owes the other the same obligations described here.

WHAT THIS MUTUAL AGREEMENT DOESN'T COVER
This agreement doesn't restrict information that was already public, that the Receiving Party already knew before receiving it from the Disclosing Party, that the Receiving Party develops independently without using the Disclosing Party's confidential information, or that the Receiving Party is required to disclose by law — though the Receiving Party will tell the Disclosing Party first if legally able to. These exclusions apply the same way to Acme, Inc. and Beta Ventures, LLC, whichever one is receiving information at the time.

CALIFORNIA'S TRADE SECRET DEFINITION
Like the parties' own definition of confidential information in this agreement, California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act has its own, separate definition of "trade secret" that applies regardless of what this contract says. Under that statute, a trade secret is information that (1) derives independent economic value from not being generally known to others who could profit from it, and (2) is the subject of efforts reasonable under the circumstances to keep it secret. Both Acme, Inc. and Beta Ventures, LLC can agree in this contract to treat a broader category of information as confidential than the statute would separately protect as a trade secret — the two are not the same thing, and this agreement's confidentiality promises don't depend on the disclosed information actually meeting the statutory test.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Trade secret” means information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process, that: (1) Derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use; and (2) Is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, definition of "trade secret" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.1.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of the state's own trade-secret definition — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this agreement or any dispute under it. The wording differs somewhat from the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's definition, which uses 'reasonable measures' rather than 'efforts reasonable under the circumstances' and separately requires that the information not be 'readily ascertainable through proper means' — the practical difference between these formulations, if any, was not tested against case law in this research. No case law interpreting this specific California definition was checked here; the statute's own text is unambiguous about the two-element test, so the statute stands as the source without a corroborating case. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 3426.1(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

THIS CONTRACT'S CONFIDENTIALITY DUTY IS SEPARATE FROM TRADE SECRET LAW
California's trade secret statute expressly does not take away or limit contractual confidentiality remedies, whether or not the information at issue would separately qualify as a trade secret. That means a breach of this agreement's confidentiality promises can be pursued as a contract claim on its own terms, without either Acme, Inc. or Beta Ventures, LLC having to first show the disclosed information met the statutory trade-secret test. Separately, California's trade secret statute sets its own three-year discovery-rule deadline for bringing a trade-secret misappropriation lawsuit — but that deadline applies only to misappropriation claims under that statute. It does not set, extend, or limit how long this agreement's own confidentiality obligations last; that duration is whatever term the parties write into this contract.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "This title does not affect (1) contractual remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, (2) other civil remedies that are not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, or (3) criminal remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, effect on other remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.7.)
  "An action for misappropriation must be brought within three years after the misappropriation is discovered or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have been discovered. For the purposes of this section, a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.6 (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, statute of limitations for misappropriation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.6.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of how that state's trade secret law relates to contract law — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this agreement. No case law applying this displacement provision to a mutual non-disclosure agreement specifically was checked in this research; the statutory text is unambiguous on its own terms about preserving contractual remedies, so the statute stands as the source here without a corroborating case. Separately: outside of trade-secret misappropriation claims specifically, there is no special statutory deadline for suing over a plain breach of a confidentiality contract — an ordinary breach-of-contract claim would instead be governed by California's general statute of limitations for written contracts, which was not independently verified in this research and is not quoted here.

WHETHER THE FEDERAL WHISTLEBLOWER NOTICE APPLIES TO A COMPANY-TO-COMPANY AGREEMENT
Federal law's whistleblower immunity notice requirement is written to apply to "any contract or agreement with an employee that governs the use of a trade secret or other confidential information," and the statute defines "employee," for purposes of that notice requirement only, to include "any individual performing work as a contractor or consultant for an employer." A mutual non-disclosure agreement between two business entities, where neither Acme, Inc.'s nor Beta Ventures, LLC's individual personnel is personally performing contractor or consultant work for the other side, sits outside that statutory language on its face — the notice mandate is framed around an individual doing work for an employer, not two companies exchanging information as counterparties. The same federal notice requirement is squarely triggered, by contrast, whenever one of the parties to a confidentiality agreement is an individual, sole proprietor, or independent contractor performing work for the other rather than a business entity dealing at arm's length.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An employer shall provide notice of the immunity set forth in this subsection in any contract or agreement with an employee that governs the use of a trade secret or other confidential information."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3)(A) (official uscode.house.gov text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, notice requirement (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title18-section1833&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "For purposes of this subsection, the term "employee" includes any individual performing work as a contractor or consultant for an employer."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(4) (official uscode.house.gov text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, definition of "employee" for the notice requirement (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title18-section1833&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: This clause cites two paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b) — (b)(3)(A) and (b)(4); no additional independent source was found for either point beyond the statute's own text. This is the federal government's statute, used as real evidence of what the notice requirement's own text covers — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this agreement. No case law was checked on how courts have resolved close cases at this boundary (for example, a sole proprietor doing business under a company name, or a company whose only "employee" is its own owner) — the statute's own text is unambiguous about the general rule, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case. This is a scoping question only, distinct from the existing one-way NDA's whistleblower-notice clause: that clause already covers the immunity's substance, the notice-and-consequence rule, the policy-document alternative, and the anti-retaliation carve-out in full, and none of that is repeated here.

TERM, SURVIVAL, AND SIGNATURES
This agreement's confidentiality obligations continue for three (3) years from the date each piece of information is disclosed. That duration is a term the parties are setting for themselves in this contract, not a period fixed by statute.

Please sign below to indicate agreement to the terms above.

Date: _______________

Beta Ventures, LLC: _______________
Date: _______________
